questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain how axon length matches target distance
questions.stem: Explain why interneurons of the brain and spinal cord can be short while motor neurons reaching the foot must be extremely long.

answer.exemplar: Interneurons only carry signals to nearby cells, so a short axon is enough, whereas a motor neuron must span from the spinal cord down to a foot muscle, so its axon grows long to bridge that distance without extra relay steps.

questions.explanation: Axon length matches the distance to the target cell, so nearby targets need short axons while distant muscles require long ones.
questions.hint: What determines how long an axon must be?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a myelinated axon conducts an impulse faster than an unmyelinated axon of the same length.

answer.exemplar: Myelin insulates the membrane so charge cannot leak out, and the impulse only regenerates at the nodes of Ranvier, letting the signal jump from node to node instead of crawling along every patch of bare membrane.

questions.explanation: Insulation reduces leakage and the saltatory jump skips most of the membrane, so fewer regeneration steps are needed per millimeter.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain a toxin's effect on signaling
questions.stem: A toxin makes voltage-gated sodium channels close much more slowly than normal. Explain why an exposed nerve produces slow, repeated bursts of signalling.

answer.exemplar: When sodium channels stay open too long, the membrane repolarizes late, so the neuron spends extra time depolarized and each recovery is stretched, letting follow-up activity pile up as slow repeated bursts.

questions.explanation: Slowed channel closing lengthens depolarization and the reset that follows, so each impulse takes longer and neighboring signals blur together.
questions.hint: Trace what the channels do at the end of the spike.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why an action potential travels in only one direction down the axon.

answer.exemplar: The segment just behind the impulse is in its refractory period and cannot fire again until its channels reset, so the wave of depolarization can only push forward into membrane that is still at rest.

questions.explanation: The refractory wake behind the impulse blocks re-firing, so the moving spike can only advance into membrane that is ready.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why a stronger-than-threshold stimulus feels more intense even though every impulse is the same size.

answer.exemplar: A stronger stimulus pushes the neuron over threshold sooner and more often, so the fiber fires at a higher rate and recruits more neighboring fibers, and the brain reads that larger volley of identical impulses as a stronger sensation.

questions.explanation: Intensity is coded by firing frequency and by the number of active fibers, not by making each individual spike taller.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain how an inhibitory synapse can veto an otherwise strong excitatory input.

answer.exemplar: An inhibitory input opens chloride or potassium channels that hold the membrane below threshold, so the excitatory depolarization is shunted and the neuron stays silent even though excitatory transmitter is present.

questions.explanation: Inhibition stabilizes the membrane, so summed excitation has to push past that clamp before any impulse can start.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Explain why the same neurotransmitter can excite one target cell and inhibit another.

answer.exemplar: A transmitter's effect depends on which receptor it binds, and receptors differ across cells, so a receptor that lets positive charge in excites one cell while a chloride-permeable receptor in another holds that cell below threshold.

questions.explanation: Different receptor subtypes on the target cell decide whether the transmitter depolarizes or stabilizes the membrane.
questions.hint: Focus on the receiving side.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: design a plan to strengthen a synapse
questions.stem: A research team wants to strengthen and prolong a synapse's signal without changing how much transmitter is released per impulse. Draft a plan and predict the risk.

answer.exemplar: Block both cleanup routes by inhibiting the reuptake transporter and the enzyme that degrades the transmitter, so the chemical stays in the cleft longer and receptors are stimulated for longer; the risk is that receptors downregulate, producing tolerance to the amplified signal.

questions.explanation: The plan targets removal rather than release, so transmitter accumulates in the cleft; the risk is receptor downregulation from overstimulation.
questions.hint: Count the ways transmitter leaves the cleft.
